Finding: The Economically Strained and Insecure segment is most prevalent among those aged 60+ (0.46 [0.39, 0.52]), differing significantly from all other age groups. The Secure Assets, High Instability segment is most prevalent among those aged 16-29 (0.59 [0.54, 0.64]), who differ from the 30-44, 45-59, and 60+ groups. For the High Vulnerability and Insecurity segment, the data only separate the 30-44 and 60+ groups.
Caution: Accounting for the survey design did not move any estimate by more than 0.004. It made the confidence intervals wider for most groups, notably 1.30 times wider for the 16-29 group in the Secure Assets, High Instability segment.

Finding: The data show that females and males differ in their composition of the Secure Assets, High Instability and Economically Strained and Insecure segments. For the High Vulnerability and Insecurity and Government-Dependent Vulnerable segments, the data do not separate the groups.
Caution: Accounting for the survey design moved estimates by at most 0.004 and made the confidence intervals wider, by factors ranging from 1.05 to 1.36 times.

Finding: Education levels differ significantly across most segments. In the Secure Assets, High Instability segment, Tertiary (0.73) is more represented than Secondary (0.49) and Primary (0.18). Conversely, the Economically Strained and Insecure segment is most represented by those with Primary education (0.45), followed by Secondary (0.19) and Tertiary (0.08). For the High Vulnerability and Insecurity segment, the data do not separate Primary (0.21) and Secondary (0.21), but both differ from Tertiary (0.14).
Caution: Accounting for the survey design moved estimates by at most 0.003 and changed the width of the intervals, for example, making the interval for the Government-Dependent Vulnerable Segment (Primary) 1.24 times as wide.

Finding: Urban and rural populations differ in their composition of the 'Secure Assets, High Instability' and 'Economically Strained and Insecure' segments. For all other segments, the data do not separate the urban and rural groups.
Caution: Accounting for the survey design did not move any estimate by more than 0.002. It made the intervals narrower for the rural 'High Vulnerability and Insecurity' segment (0.79 times as wide) and wider for all other groups, ranging from 1.13 to 1.41 times as wide.

Finding: The Unemployed are more likely to be in the High Vulnerability and Insecurity segment than any other employment group. Students are significantly more likely to be in the Secure Assets, High Instability segment than any other group. In the Economically Strained and Insecure segment, Homemakers are more likely to be present than Students or the Unemployed.
Caution: Accounting for the survey design did not move any estimate by more than 0.007. The design generally made the confidence intervals wider, with the largest increase being 1.19 times for the Unemployed in the Economically Strained and Insecure segment.
